reading.identification: An early-20th-century eclectic/Beaux-Arts corner commercial-residential house at the Korenmarkt/Hooiaard corner in Ghent — four storeys of painted render over masonry, banded at ground level, with a first-floor wrought-iron balcony and an arched piano-nobile opening, its ground floor now occupied by the Wasbar laundry-café.
reading.notes:
EVIDENCE SPLIT. Seen in B (close range, though at the frame edge under wide-lens curvature): painted smooth render walls, horizontally channelled/banded render at ground level, full-width first-floor balcony on black wrought-iron railing carried on consoles, string-course band between ground and first floor, round-arched opening above the balcony, tall metal-framed shopfront glazing of the Wasbar laundry-cafe (AEG machine and neon lettering legible through the glass). Seen in A: four storey bands, regular bay rhythm, white/cream colour, presence of a pitched (non-flat) dark roof and an eaves cornice line. Inferred: window dimensions, glazing subdivision, roof form, and the metre heights.

HEIGHTS ARE DERIVED, NOT SEEN. Storey count is read from A; the metre values are back-solved from the measured height_m 15.8 so they close against it: 4.2 (tall commercial ground floor, consistent with the double-height-reading Wasbar glazing) + 3 x 3.3 = 14.1 m to eaves, leaving ~1.7 m of roof above the cornice. Do not treat 4.2/3.3 as observed.

ROOF IS THE WEAKEST FIELD. B is cut off above the first floor (the outline runs off the top of the frame), so the roof is invisible from the pavement exactly as warned. A shows a dark pitched mass with an eaves line but at ~25 cm/texel cannot separate mansard from hipped. Mansard with the ridge parallel to Hooiaard is the period-and-place prior for a Korenmarkt corner block of this date; ~1.7 m of roof height suits a mansard whose lower slope hides behind the cornice. If a roof dataset exists, it overrides this outright.

BAY COUNT. 9.0 m frontage over 4 bays gives a 2.25 m module — 1.2 m opening on a 1.05 m pier, which is the rhythm A shows. The 7.5 x 11.2 footprint with street_frontages 2 means this is a corner unit; the 9.0 m figure and this grammar describe the Hooiaard elevation that both plates actually see. The return elevation should inherit the same storey bands and string course but not necessarily the balcony.

PHYSICS REGIMES. Above 10 cm, build as geometry: the balcony slab, its consoles and the iron balustrade (the strongest scatterer on this facade and the one feature that most changes street-level field on a 12 m-wide pedestrian canyon), window reveals at the shallow class, sills, the string course, the eaves cornice, and the shopfront frame. 1-10 cm — the channelled render banding at ground level, any ornament around the arch — must NOT be meshed; it is carried by the roughness number. Painted smooth render is genuinely smooth, hence 1.0 mm RMS; the banding grooves are shallow and sparse and do not justify pushing it toward a brick-like 3-8 mm. Wall is set to concrete as the standard proxy for render over masonry (the render is the surface the ray sees, not the brick behind it); trim is metal for the balustrade and shopfront framing, both directly visible.

CLUTTER — CHECK THE ACCESS TAG. fronting_street is pedestrian, surface sett, car_access none. Place NO vehicles on Hooiaard. The correct clutter, all of it visible in B, is cafe terrace furniture directly against this facade (timber tables, black metal chairs), folded parasols on masts, planters, bollards, and a tactile paving strip with embedded tram rails crossing the sett. Terrace furniture sits within 2 m of the wall and is worth explicit geometry here; it is between the beam and the facade.

DETAIL BUDGET. This building is at distance_m 0.0 from the corridor, so it earns the full budget — concentrate it on the balcony assembly, the ground-floor glazing plane and its reveals, and the silhouette at the cornice. Do not spend equally on the return elevation or the roof slopes, which no plate resolves.
